title: CenterNet: Keypoint Triplets for Object Detection

problem.summary: The paper shows that keypoint-based one-stage detectors such as CornerNet produce a large number of incorrect bounding boxes because they never look inside the predicted regions, and that anchor-based detectors rely on many manually designed, poorly aligned anchors.
statements: Keypoint-based detectors emit many incorrect boxes: CornerNet reaches a 32.7% false discovery rate even at IoU 0.05, and 60.3% for small objects.
CornerNet cannot look into the regions inside its bounding boxes because it removes the RoI extraction process.

Anchor-based detectors need many anchors to reach a high IoU with ground truth, and each anchor's size and aspect ratio must be manually designed while anchors are usually not aligned with ground-truth boxes.

evidence.quote: In object detection, keypoint-based approaches often suffer a large number of incorrect object bounding boxes, arguably due to the lack of an additional look into the cropped regions.
One of the possible reasons lies in that CornerNet cannot look into the regions inside the bounding boxes.

These approaches often need a large number of anchors to ensure a sufficiently high IoU (intersection over union) rate with the ground-truth objects, and the size and aspect ratio of each anchor box need to be manually designed.
CornerNet obtains 32.7% FD rate at IoU = 0.05.

background.summary: The work builds directly on CornerNet's corner-keypoint one-stage detector and on the two-stage vs one-stage taxonomy of deep detection; the gap claimed is that CornerNet has no mechanism to inspect the content of its own predicted boxes, while a two-stage RoI-pooling fix would be too expensive.

evidence.quote: object detection approaches can be roughly categorized into two main types of pipelines, namely, two-stage approaches and one-stage approaches.
The keypoint-based object detection approaches [40, 28] are proposed to avoid the disadvantages of using anchor boxes and bounding boxes regression.

solution.summary: CenterNet represents each object as a triplet of keypoints (top-left corner, bottom-right corner, center), keeps a candidate box only if a same-class center keypoint falls inside a scale-aware central region, and enriches the center and corner features with center pooling and cascade corner pooling.
solution.approach: Add a center-keypoint branch to CornerNet and validate each predicted box by checking whether a center keypoint of the same class lies in its scale-aware central region, rescoring the box with the three keypoint scores.
components: center keypoint heatmap branch alongside the two corner heatmaps
scale-aware central region (n = 3 or 5 depending on box scale)
center pooling: max summed response in horizontal and vertical directions
cascade corner pooling: boundary maximum plus internal maximum
triplet score = average of top-left, bottom-right and center scores
Soft-NMS and top-100 box selection at inference

evidence.quote: Our approach, named CenterNet, detects each object as a triplet, rather than a pair, of keypoints, which improves both precision and recall.
The idea, as shown in Figure 1, is to use a triplet, instead of a pair, of keypoints to represent each object.
if a center keypoint is detected in the central region, we will preserve the bounding box.
The second strategy is named cascade corner pooling, which equips the original corner pooling module [20] with the ability of perceiving internal information.
To address this issue, we propose center pooling to capture richer and more recognizable visual patterns.

experiments.summary: The method is trained on MS-COCO trainval35k and evaluated on test-dev with AP/AR, then analysed with a false-discovery metric, component ablations (central region, center pooling, cascade corner pooling), an error analysis using ground-truth centers, and an inference-speed test on a Tesla P100.

evidence.quote: On the MS-COCO dataset, CenterNet achieves an AP of 47.0%, which outperforms all existing one-stage detectors by at least 4.9%.
reports a single-scale testing AP of 41.6%, an improvement of 3.8% over 37.8%, and a multi-scale testing AP of 43.5%,
Table 3 shows the FD rates for CornerNet and CenterNet.

limitations.summary: Detection quality hinges on predicting the center keypoint: a missed center keypoint disables the whole region-inspection mechanism, and substituting ground-truth centers lifts AP by roughly 15 points, showing center keypoint detection is far from solved.
items: If the center keypoint is not detected, the visual patterns inside the box are never examined and the box is dropped.
Replacing predicted center keypoints with ground truth raises AP from 41.3% to 56.5% (Hourglass-52), indicating large remaining headroom in center keypoint detection.
Two-stage competitors typically feed higher-resolution inputs, which helps them especially on small objects.

evidence.quote: In other words, once a center keypoint is missed, the proposed CenterNet would miss the visual patterns within the bounding box.
the results suggest there is still room for improvement in detecting center keypoints.
The exploration of visual patterns within each bounding box depends on the center keypoints.

futureDirections.direction: Generalize the extra center-keypoint branch to other one-stage detectors such as SSD.
futureDirections.quote: We believe that our idea of adding an extra branch for the center keypoint can be potentially generalized to other existing one-stage approaches (e.g., SSD [27]).

futureDirections.direction: Adopt advanced training strategies to improve performance.
futureDirections.quote: Meanwhile, some advanced training strategies [46] can be used for better performance. We leave as our future work.

deploymentClaims: Average inference of 270ms per image with the Hourglass-52 backbone and 340ms with Hourglass-104, measured on an NVIDIA Tesla P100 GPU
Implemented in PyTorch and trained from scratch on 8 Tesla V100 (32GB) GPUs with batch size 48

evidence.quote: To ensure a fair comparison, we test the inference speed of both CornerNet [20] and CenterNet on a NVIDIA Tesla P100 GPU.
Our CenterNet511-52 takes an average of 270ms to process per image, which is faster and more accurate than CornerNet511-104.
